title: A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a neural interface that maintains useful two-way communication between a person’s nervous system and an assistive device for years. It would decode intended actions into commands and deliver sensory information back to neural tissue. In the envisioned use, a person with paralysis or limb loss could control an assistive limb while receiving information about contact and movement. This is a synthesis of the proposed concept.

Durability would encompass the continuing usefulness of the whole system, including neural recordings, decoding, sensory stimulation, and adaptation to the user’s changing needs. Bidirectional function would require the person to interpret and use the returned information during action. The proposed capability therefore combines sustained control with useful sensory feedback in everyday tasks. These are conceptual requirements supplied for this innovation.

significance.text: If achieved, the interface could provide a practical communication channel between the nervous system and the world after paralysis or limb loss. Combining intended-action decoding with contact and movement feedback could help users adjust an assistive device during interaction with objects. The revolutionary potential lies in sustaining that combined capability through years of ordinary use. These consequences follow conditionally from the proposed breakthrough.

Further possibilities include more independent assistive-device use and a reduced need to monitor every action visually, provided that the feedback is timely, interpretable, and useful. The extent of those benefits would depend on the task, the person’s condition, and the device being controlled. Natural-feeling sensation, restored biological movement, and broad clinical availability would each require additional evidence and potentially further advances. These are conditional implications and limits identified through conceptual review.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed unsolved capability is sustained, practical motor-and-sensory communication over years despite changes in neural tissue, recorded signals, and user needs. The supplied research identifies biological reactions around the interface and signal drift as barriers. As an engineering synthesis, these problems require maintaining a usable tissue–device connection while keeping the relationship between neural activity and intended action sufficiently dependable for everyday control. Their precise contribution to performance loss is unverified in the supplied evidence.

Sensory encoding presents a separate challenge. The interface must translate information such as contact and limb position into neural stimulation that the user can interpret and apply during movement. A convincing system would need to coordinate this feedback with decoded commands, sustain its usefulness as conditions change, and manage the calibration and maintenance needed to preserve function. These are proposed engineering requirements inferred from the concept, with no inspectable technical source supplied to establish their current solutions or remaining limits.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a report titled “Long-term independent use of an intracortical brain–computer interface for speech and cursor control” to Nicholas S. Card and colleagues, dated 15 June 2026, with DOI 10.1038/s41591-026-04414-6. It describes one man with paralysis using speech and cursor decoders independently at home, without researchers present, for more than 3,800 hours over nearly two years. These bibliographic and performance details remain attributed claims because the retained source did not permit their verification.

The retained material for that URL contains only a cookie-access notice and provides no inspectable abstract or scientific text. Consequently, the publication’s identity, authorship, date, participant count, usage hours, duration, and conditions of independent operation could not be confirmed through the supplied review. The earlier statement that the abstract had been inspected exceeds what the retained material establishes. This access limitation leaves the reported result unresolved.

If confirmed, the reported speech-and-cursor performance would demonstrate a substantial component of long-term usefulness and independent output control. Establishing the proposed innovation would additionally require evidence of useful sensory input integrated with movement control over comparable periods. The supplied material provides no verified demonstration of that combined capability and no basis for assessing developments after the attributed June 2026 report. This is an assessment of the supplied evidence’s scope.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing demonstration would involve multiple users independently operating the interface in everyday life for years, completing varied tasks while receiving useful touch and position feedback. A protocol would need to define independence, specify permitted caregiver and technical assistance, and report how often calibration, troubleshooting, or researcher intervention occurs. These are proposed evaluation criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple users independently perform everyday tasks with feedback for years

completion_criteria.text: Sensory usefulness should be demonstrated through its contribution to task performance and the user’s ability to interpret contact and movement information. A proposed evaluation could compare performance with feedback enabled and disabled, while also comparing function, safety, and maintenance burden with relevant existing assistive devices. Longitudinal reporting should make changes in control quality, feedback usefulness, and support requirements visible across the study period. These comparisons are proposals for testing the intended capability.
completion_criteria.label: Sensory feedback demonstrates usefulness through task performance and interpretation

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility would require consistent findings across users and independent teams, with the tested conditions and practical boundaries clearly described. Reports should identify the supported tasks, user populations, environments, device configurations, and duration of successful operation. Finite demonstrations could establish breadth within those boundaries. Any claim of generality would remain limited by the populations, tasks, and time periods actually studied. These are proposed evidentiary expectations.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce consistent findings across users within stated boundaries

related_concepts.text: BME-03, Reconstruction of a chronically severed spinal cord, shares the objective of recovering function after paralysis. BME-04 proposes an engineered communication pathway between neural tissue and an assistive system. BME-03 centers on reconstruction of the spinal cord itself. Their relationship is potentially complementary, and each requires its own evidence of functional recovery. This comparison is a synthesis based on the supplied concept descriptions.

BME-16, Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants, overlaps directly with the durability of the neural tissue–device connection. Improvements in integration could contribute to BME-04, whose completion also requires intended-action decoding and useful sensory encoding. BME-18, Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers, shares challenges of sustained signal quality and long-term operation, with its primary output directed toward physiological measurement. These distinctions are conceptual inferences from the supplied roster.

BME-13, Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement, shares the broader engineering demands of dependable long-term function and manageable maintenance. BME-04 specifically concerns communication with the nervous system for control and sensation. BME-10, Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use, could intersect with individualized interface planning or evaluation, but that connection is a conditional possibility inferred from its title. Neither concept’s completion would by itself establish a durable bidirectional neural interface.

unresolved_issues: The identity and contents of the publication associated with the supplied PubMed URL remain unverified, including its authorship, date, DOI, participant count, usage hours, duration, and conditions of independent home use.
No inspectable scientific source in the supplied material establishes the present solutions or remaining limits for biological reactions, signal drift, changing user needs, and sensory encoding.
The supplied evidence does not establish a years-long demonstration combining movement control with useful touch and position feedback.
The bounded freshness record is empty, leaving the state of the field as of November 2026 unassessed.
Operational definitions and quantitative thresholds for independence, useful feedback, acceptable safety, and manageable maintenance remain to be specified in a future evaluation protocol.

brief.title: Years of reliable control and feeling in an assistive limb
possible: People with paralysis or limb loss could control an assistive limb and feel when it touches objects and how it moves, with the system remaining useful for years. It would turn intended actions into device commands and send sensory information back to the nervous system.
why: Useful feedback could help people adjust their grip and movements while handling objects. Sustaining that connection could make assistive devices more practical for independent daily use and reduce the need to watch every action.

sources.showed: A man with paralysis used brain signals to communicate and control a computer independently at home for nearly two years. A care partner helped with putting on and removing the hardware and starting the software.
sources.quote: He labeled 92% of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.
sources.cited_for: The study supports lasting, independent use of brain signals for communication and computer control.
sources.not_established: It did not demonstrate movement control combined with useful touch and position feedback.

sources.showed: A person with paralysis controlled a robotic arm through brain signals. Adding touch sensations through brain stimulation roughly halved task completion times, mainly by making grasping faster.
sources.quote: Faster times were primarily due to less time spent attempting to grasp objects, revealing that mimicking known biological control principles results in task performance that is closer to healthy human abilities.
sources.cited_for: Touch feedback improved practical object handling with a brain-controlled arm.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish years of independent everyday use across users.

sources.showed: A small take-home study tested artificial arms that returned touch sensations to people with limb loss. Touch changed how participants used their arms, while longer-term changes in task performance varied.
sources.quote: The presence of touch sensation had a near-immediate impact on how the users operated their prostheses.
sources.cited_for: Home use can change both practical performance and how users perceive an artificial limb as part of their body.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish consistently improved everyday function with useful touch and position feedback across users.

sources.showed: In a preprint, a participant being evaluated for epilepsy surgery used brain signals to control a walking device and receive leg sensations. The system also ran on portable computing hardware.
sources.quote: Finally, we demonstrated that all BDBCI operations can be executed on a dedicated, portable embedded system.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates combined walking control and leg sensory feedback.
sources.not_established: It did not establish lasting independent use by people with paralysis.

shown: Card and colleagues demonstrated independent home communication and computer control for nearly two years in a man with paralysis. Flesher and colleagues showed that adding touch sensations made robotic-arm tasks faster in a participant with paralysis.

Schofield and colleagues studied touch-enabled artificial arms at home, with varied changes in performance. Lim and colleagues demonstrated walking control with leg sensations in a preprint involving a participant undergoing epilepsy evaluation.
missing: Movement control and useful touch and position feedback still need to work together for years in everyday life.
The whole system must remain useful as tissue responses, neural signals and users’ needs change.
Multiple users must sustain practical independence with manageable calibration, maintenance and technical support.
Independent teams must reproduce consistent benefits within clearly stated conditions.

milestones.label: Multiple users complete everyday tasks with feedback for years
milestones.explanation: Multiple users would have to complete varied everyday tasks independently for years with useful touch and position feedback, while reporting assistance and upkeep. This would establish lasting practical use.

milestones.label: Sensory feedback improves tasks and conveys understandable information
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show that users understand feedback and perform better with it, alongside comparisons with existing devices and tracking of safety and upkeep. This would establish useful sensation during action.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce consistent results across users
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce consistent findings across users, specifying tasks, settings, devices and duration. This would establish where the capability reliably works.

uncertain: How much do tissue reactions and changing neural signals limit lasting control and sensation?
What levels of assistance, safety and maintenance would count as practical independence?
How reliably will users interpret touch and position feedback as their needs and the system change?

page.title: Bidirectional sensorimotor neural interfaces for home use
page.definition: An implanted interface lets a person with paralysis or limb loss control an assistive limb and receive touch or limb-position information through neural stimulation during home use over years. Bidirectional means that motor commands flow out and sensory information flows back.

goal.need: WHO estimated that 15.4 million people lived with spinal cord injury in 2021, a condition that can impair movement and sensation. In one participant with tetraplegia, adding cortical touch feedback reduced median robotic-arm task time from 20.9 s to 10.2 s. Retaining that sensory contribution alongside movement control during home use is the capability sought.

figures.caption: Robotic-arm task performance in one participant, published on 21 May 2021.
figures.note: Each condition comprised four sessions and 108 attempted trials using a modified Action Research Arm Test. Trial counts are repeated observations from one participant.

statements.quote: developing new high-performance neural interfaces that last the life of the patient.
statements.context: The programme page is undated. The year identifies the programme's launch.

statements.body: DARPA, Hand Proprioception and Touch Interfaces programme
statements.quote: The ultimate goal is to create a fully-implantable device that is safe, reliable, effective, and approved for human use.

completion.title: An implanted motor–sensory limb interface receives FDA approval for multiyear home use.
completion.criterion: FDA grants premarket approval to a complete implanted system whose approved intended use includes home operation with decoded limb control and sensor-driven neural sensory feedback over a multiyear service life. The approval order, approved labelling and safety-and-effectiveness summary establish the authorised population, functions, operating conditions and supporting durability evidence. Performance margins, participant numbers and duration requirements are those accepted by FDA for that device.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback using DARPA's HAPTIX goal and FDA's premarket approval pathway.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA implanted-BCI guidance and approval criteria, DARPA HAPTIX and RE-NET targets, IEEE standards and trial registries found no single published test combining multiyear durability, limb control, neural sensation and home use. The Atlas adopts marketing approval for that combined indication, following DARPA's stated human-approval goal. Device-specific requirements come from the regulator.

milestones.title: An implanted interface demonstrates motor–sensory function and supports first human testing.
milestones.criterion: Bench and animal evaluations support preliminary safety for the proposed human study, including recording, stimulation and tissue effects under intended operating conditions. FDA makes sample size, model and duration device-specific. A cortical laboratory result published on 5 October 2011 showed two monkeys using decoded movements and cortical stimulation to distinguish three visually identical objects. That result demonstrates closed-loop task function within this stage.
milestones.set_by: FDA, implanted-BCI guidance, Animal Studies section. These are nonbinding, device-specific recommendations.

milestones.title: A human study demonstrates limb control with neural sensory feedback and initial clinical safety.
milestones.criterion: An authorised early-feasibility study provides proof of principle and initial clinical safety data for movement control with sensory return. Cortical results include Flesher's one-person robotic-arm study, published on 21 May 2021, and Lim's one-person exoskeleton study, published on 28 February 2026, with 92.8% blind step-counting accuracy. Cady's peripheral implant study, published on 23 April 2025, enrolled two participants and demonstrated prosthesis control in one. The other participant's implant was removed after four months because of infection.
milestones.set_by: FDA, guidance on early-feasibility medical-device studies. This defines the clinical stage without a universal numerical safety threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: A complete bidirectional limb system undergoes 12 months of take-home clinical use.
milestones.criterion: The complete motor-and-sensory limb system undergoes 12 months of take-home clinical use. Peripheral evidence includes a report of four implanted users, three followed for 3–7 years, with touch feedback introduced later in January 2017 for one and September 2018 for two, published on 30 April 2020. Related reinnervated-skin systems supplied touch for two home users over two years, with one control, published on 19 February 2020. Cortical output durability is supported by Card's one-person speech-and-cursor study over nearly two years after caregiver setup, published on 15 June 2026.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, HAPTIX programme culmination target. The published target concerns peripheral upper-limb prostheses. Its application to central interfaces is an Atlas extension.
milestones.threshold_quote: DARPA anticipates a 12-month, take-home clinical trial of the complete HAPTIX system as the culmination of the program.

milestones.title: FDA finds a bidirectional home-use system's marketing application approvable.
milestones.criterion: FDA issues an approvable letter for the complete system's premarket approval application, finding that it substantially meets statutory requirements and identifying the additional information or conditions needed for approval. The clinical evidence addresses the combined motor-and-sensory home-use indication. FDA's implanted-BCI guidance recommends at least one year of follow-up. Participant counts and numerical safety and effectiveness success margins remain protocol-specific.
milestones.set_by: FDA, PMA Review Process, Approvable Letter section, under 21 CFR 814.44(e).
milestones.threshold_quote: FDA will send the applicant an approvable letter if the application substantially meets the requirements of the FD&C Act,

not_found: No public pivotal protocol with numerical success criteria for the combined multiyear motor-and-sensory home-use indication was located.
A multiyear cortical home-use demonstration combining limb control and neural sensory feedback was not located.

results.finding: One participant used an intracortical speech-and-cursor BCI at home for 19 months.
results.detail: Care partners assisted with setup. The system did not control an assistive limb or provide neural sensory feedback, so it was not a complete bidirectional limb system.
results.quote: With care partner assistance largely restricted to donning and doffing the hardware and initializing the software, a man with paralysis and severe dysarthria due to ALS used the system in his home nearly every day for 19 months, accumulating more than 3,800 h of independent use.

results.finding: One participant controlled a robotic arm with cortical tactile feedback, reducing median trial time by 51.2%.
results.detail: The study was conducted under an FDA investigational device exemption and demonstrates motor control with sensory feedback, but the supplied text does not report clinical safety outcomes.
results.quote: This enabled a person with tetraplegia to substantially improve performance with a robotic limb; trial times on a clinical upper-limb assessment were reduced by half, from a median time of 20.9 to 10.2 s.

results.finding: Three participants tested myoelectric prostheses with touch feedback.
results.detail: Motor signals were recorded from reinnervated muscles, and tactors stimulated reinnervated skin. The study does not report an implanted interface or initial clinical safety data.
results.quote: We recruited three participants with high-level upper-limb amputation who previously received targeted reinnervation surgery. Each participant was fit with a neural-machine-interface prosthesis that allowed participants to operate their device by thinking about moving their missing limb.

results.finding: Two participants had touch-enabled prosthetic arms at home for 2 years.
results.detail: The system used surface electrodes and tactors on reinnervated skin rather than an implanted interface. Diary coverage was incomplete, and reported wear in the final two months averaged under 6 hours per week.
results.quote: SD had her touch-enabled arm for 2 years and we received activity diaries for 25 weeks. During the 2-month period immediately before her final visit, she wore the arm for an average of 4.9 ± 3.7 h per week. TH also had her touch-enabled arm for 2 years

results.finding: One participant used a brain–computer interface for walking control with bilateral leg sensory feedback.
results.detail: The participant was undergoing electrode implantation for epilepsy evaluation. The excerpt does not establish an authorised early-feasibility study or report initial clinical safety data for the complete system.
results.quote: Here, a subject undergoing subdural electrocorticogram electrode implantation for epilepsy surgery evaluation leveraged the leg representation areas of the bilateral interhemispheric primary motor and sensory cortices to operate a BDBCI with high performance.

results.finding: Two implanted monkeys used cortical motor control and sensory stimulation to distinguish one of three visually identical objects.
results.detail: The study demonstrated closed-loop motor–sensory task function, but the supplied text does not report the tissue-effects and preliminary safety evaluations needed to support a proposed human study.
results.quote: Two monkeys operated this BMBI to search and discriminate one out of three visually undistinguishable objects, using the virtual hand to identify the unique artificial texture (AT) associated with each.

results.finding: iSens implanted peripheral system, sample size not stated: saline recordings showed negligible stimulus artifact 10 cm from a 1 mA source.

results.finding: Two participants received peripheral implants; one controlled a prosthesis in 3 degrees of freedom with sensory feedback.
results.detail: The study was conducted under an FDA Investigational Device Exemption. The second participant’s implant was removed after 15 weeks because of infection; the first required revision surgery after a lead failure.
results.quote: Using an artificial neural network controller trained on implanted electromyographic data collected during known hand movements, one participant commanded a virtual hand and sensorized prosthesis in 3 degrees-of-freedom. The iSens® system simultaneously produced stimulation for sensation while recording high resolution muscle activity for real-time control.

results.finding: In one participant, 60% of sensory electrodes remained functional after 10 years.
results.detail: This supports long-term sensory-component durability, but the study does not report 12 months of take-home use of a complete bidirectional limb system. Stimulation occurred intermittently in monitored sessions.
results.quote: This proportion decreased over time: After 4 years, 80 and 75% of the electrodes for participants C1 and P3 were functional, respectively, whereas after 10 years, 60% of participant P2’s electrodes were functional.
